title: What is the Most Pointless Thing You Do as an Educator?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart asks teachers to name the task least likely to promote students' long-term flourishing, listing his own: micro-grading with overwhelming rubrics, most email, evaluation-rubric minutiae and credential upkeep. He stresses that doing these things does not make anyone a bad person, since the system itself rewards complexity and busyness. Rather than stopping at griping, he offers three options (don't do it, do it when there's time, satisfice it) and recommends satisficing: doing the task with minimal time and effort. He illustrates with the evaluation rubric, where he engages charitably with colleagues but saves real energy for the big questions, and with his choice of an affordable online master's program. The piece is a workload and sustainability argument for the profession.
points: Naming your most pointless task gives a visceral entry point into questioning how professional effort is spent.
The system pays lip service to simplicity while rewarding doing more, so the problem is partly systemic rather than personal.
Satisficing means giving minimal effort to low-value required tasks so full effort can go to the biggest questions of student growth.
Satisficing can coexist with respect for colleagues and administrators who are also bound by requirements.
quotes: We work in a system that pays lip service to the importance of ideas like simplicity, “working smarter not harder,” and reflection, yet all the while this system exalts complexity, “doing more is doing better,” and ceaseless, mindless striving. So when we engage in (or require that others engage in) pointless tasks, we are only part of the problem — the other part is systemic.

Too often, this is where the conversation stops — we sit and fixate on the mindless minutiae, lament the present state of the teaching profession, and slog on into our day. The result is demotivation, frustration, and steps down the path of the non-flourishing life.

Since I want you to keep your job, I’m going to officially recommend Option #3 — satisficing the thing. I’ve already written a brief overview on satisficing for teachers, but the gist is that we do the thing with the minimal amount of time and effort possible.

The pursuit of the biggest questions — e.g., How do I make kids grow as much as possible in the areas of thinking, reading, writing, speaking/listening, and becoming better people — get every ounce of professional effort and care that I have. But contemplation of the difference between Highly Effective and Effective on Formative Assessment Element 1b…. no. Just no.

In other words, I actively engage with the ultimate mission of the school, I continuously strive to respect and love my colleagues, and yet I merely satisfice areas where the overly complicated teacher evaluation rubric is concerned. I’m not giving you a blank check to disregard people or to belittle the tough situations administrators are put in these days, but I am insisting that you prize the most worthy intellectual work and satisfice the rest.
